title: Distributed Entanglement Distribution Using Multiple Entanglement Sources in WDM-based Quantum Optical Networks
authors: Anuj Agrawal, Abhay Singh Dulta, Bhaskar Kanseri
abstract: Quantum network implementations using single spontaneous parametric downconversion (SPDC)-based broadband entangled photon pair source (EPPS) have been reported recently. Here, leveraging the wavelength-correlation between entangled photon pairs, the traditional wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) method is utilized to route photons based on their wavelengths. From single EPPS, entangled photon pairs are distributed in a centralized way to different node pairs in the network. However, the number of nodes pairs that can be entangled in a network is limited by the number of entangled wavelength pairs that an EPPS can generate. To entangle a higher number of node pairs in a network, multiple EPPSs can be employed. In this work, we present a WDM-based entanglement distribution approach using multiple EPPSs in multi-hop repeaterless mesh optical networks. We experimentally characterize two EPPSs developed in-house and consider multiple such EPPSs in the network to perform network-level simulations. We consider heterogeneous entanglement demands requiring different entanglement bit (ebit) rates and entanglement visibility. For each entanglement demand, EPPS placement/selection, wavelength-pair assignment, and photon pair routing are performed considering the degradation in both ebit rate and visibility with fiber length and hops in the network. Two main findings of this study include: (i) a hybrid approach of one-photon (OP) and both-photon (BP) entanglement distribution provides higher flexibility in multi-EPPS placement and (ii) distributed entanglement distribution using multiple EPPSs enables better entanglement resource utilization and higher entanglement demand acceptance as compared to centralized entanglement distribution.
summary: This work proposes a method to enhance entanglement distribution in complex quantum optical networks by employing multiple distributed Entanglement Photon Pair Sources (EPPSs). By simulating performance across various mesh topologies and comparing centralized versus decentralized source placement, the authors demonstrate that distributing sources significantly boosts network capacity and resource efficiency. This advances the feasibility of building large-scale, repeaterless quantum communication links.
main_problem: The study addresses the challenge of distributing entanglement across large, multi-hop quantum optical networks without relying on quantum repeaters.
main_result: Distributed entanglement distribution using multiple Entanglement Photon Pair Sources (EPPSs) significantly outperforms centralized sources by improving resource utilization and accepting higher network demands.
method: The authors simulate network performance by comparing different EPPS placement strategies (centralized vs. distributed) across various topologies, considering One-Photon (OP) and Both-Photon (BP) distribution schemes.
model_or_system: The system is a Wavelength Division Multiplexing (WDM)-based quantum optical network utilizing multiple SPDC-based EPPSs in repeaterless mesh topologies (e.g., 7-PMESH).
key_observables: Entanglement Demand Acceptance Ratio (EDAR), Entanglement Resource Utilization Ratio (ERUR), and entanglement visibility/ebit rate degradation.
important_parameters: Fiber length, number of hops, EPPS placement strategy (centralized vs. distributed), and the type of entanglement distribution scheme (OP/BP).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a passive WDM approach without quantum repeaters; performance metrics are derived from simulated coincidence counts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate EDAR vs. Network Load curves comparing different EPPS placements in mesh networks, and ERUR comparisons showing the benefit of distributed placement.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitations of single-source entanglement distribution, then introducing the multi-EPPS WDM approach, followed by detailed comparative analysis using graph theory concepts (centrality) to optimize EPPS placement for maximizing EDAR and ERUR.
why_interesting: It provides concrete simulation results on scaling quantum network capabilities beyond simple point-to-point links, which is crucial for realizing large-scale quantum internet infrastructure.
